name: Political Asylum (Presidential Discretion)

requirements.blocker_text: Uzbekistan is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and has no comprehensive domestic asylum law. A narrow 'political asylum' mechanism exists only via a 2017 Presidential Decree and Articles 8-10 of the 2021 Law on Foreigners. The President holds sole decision-making authority, with no transparent criteria and no judicial review of a denial. The Criminal Code does shield irregular entrants seeking asylum from criminal prosecution for the entry itself, but grants no protection against deportation or refoulement.

evidence_required.document: Application demonstrating grounds for political asylum

outcome.duration_length: indefinite if granted; no defined process timeline

sources.title: Global Detention Project -- Uzbekistan's non-party status to the 1951 Convention, the narrow presidential political-asylum mechanism (2017 decree, 2021 Law on Foreigners Articles 8-10), absence of refoulement protection, and documented mistreatment of Afghan asylum seekers post-2021 including detained Afghan military pilots

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Uzbekistan). STATUS: DRAFT -- sourced to a single tier-4 human-rights-monitoring NGO; no UNHCR Uzbekistan-specific operational page was successfully fetched in this build (unhcr.org/central-asia and help.unhcr.org pages both returned fetch errors). STARK FINDING, ONE OF THE NARROWEST ASYLUM FRAMEWORKS BUILT IN THIS DATASET: unlike Kazakhstan and Montenegro's genuinely functioning systems built elsewhere in this dataset (defined timelines, court appeal rights), Uzbekistan's mechanism is sole-executive, criteria-free, and carries no refoulement protection -- worse even than Kuwait's confirmed total absence of any domestic asylum law, because Uzbekistan has SOME mechanism on paper while providing essentially none of the substantive protections the mechanism's existence might imply. The documented case of Afghan military pilots held in a 'prison-like' facility after fleeing the 2021 Taliban takeover, and hundreds of unrecognized Afghan asylum seekers more broadly, is disclosed as a specific, sourced illustration of this gap, not a generalized characterization. As of January 2025 (per the source), UNHCR recorded only 5 mandate refugees and roughly 8,500 people in refugee-like situations in the country -- small numbers that likely reflect the system's narrowness rather than low need. Uzbekistan's government has separately signaled openness to eventually acceding to the Refugee Convention (per a UNHCR Central Asia news item referenced in search results but not independently fetched for this file) -- disclosed as a stated intention only, not a current legal reality.
